results.title: Expert-centered Evaluation of Deep Learning Algorithms for Brain Tumor Segmentation - PMC
results.content: To present results from a literature survey on practices in deep learning segmentation algorithm evaluation and perform a study on expert quality perception of brain tumor segmentation. Current practices for the evaluation of deep learning models for brain tumor segmentation did not reflect the segmentation quality perception of clinical experts. * ■ Only 2.8% (five of 180 articles) of the evaluated literature on deep learning models for brain tumor segmentation included an evaluation of segmentation quality performed by clinical experts. * ■ The metric most commonly used to evaluate segmentation performance, the Dice score, showed a poor correlation with the segmentation quality perception of clinical experts (Kendall tau, 0.23) in the experimental study. We reviewed studies on DL segmentation models for brain tumors and assessed which quantitative metrics are used and whether clinical experts were involved in evaluating the algorithms’ performance. Second, we performed an experimental study to assess *(a)* interrater variability in segmentation quality perception and *(b)* variability in the agreement between quantitative metrics and experts’ quality perception for segmentations of postoperative glioblastomas. ***Quantitative evaluation of segmentation model performance.—***Among the 180 articles reviewed, the three most popular strategies to evaluate segmentation quality were the Dice score as the only evaluation metric (42 of 180 articles; 23.3%); a combination of Dice score, Hausdorff distance, sensitivity, and specificity (26 of 180 articles; 14.4%); or a combination of Dice score and Hausdorff distance (21 of 180 articles; 11.7%). While a few articles included qualitative evaluation performed by clinical experts, none linked quantitative and qualitative segmentation quality measurements. Studies including Segmentation Model Performance Evaluation by Quantitative Metrics and Clinical Experts. Upon quantitative comparison between cases with a low and high disagreement between the experts, the following factors showed statistically significant associations with a lower agreement between experts: higher segmentation volume of the automatic segmentation (*P* = .04), lower Dice score (*P* < .001), higher 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (*P* = .046) between the automatic and the manual ground truth segmentation, and a higher segmentation uncertainty of the segmentation model (*P* < .001). Second, we performed an experimental study on clinical experts’ perception of brain tumor segmentation and showed how current evaluation practices identified in the literature review relate to clinical experts’ segmentation quality assessment.

results.title: Loss, Cost, Objective Functions and Metrics | by Bhagabat Behera | Medium
results.content: # Loss, Cost, Objective Functions and Metrics. This article explains the differences among Loss function, Cost function, Objective function and evaluation metrics. Please note that the first three functions are often interchanebly used. However to differentiate them technically here are the definitions. ### **Loss Function**. It is a differentiable function that calculates loss or error for a training record. It is used for training a model using optimization techniques such as Gradient Descent. L2 loss or squared error for *a single record* with ground truth value y and predicted value y\_hat. Note: There are many loss functions used by various alogorithms and we have shown L2 loss only here. ### **Cost Function**. It is the average error for all the records in the training set calculated by the loss function. L2 loss is calculated for all the records in the training set and then the average is taken. ### Objective Function. Reducing the error is not the only purpose. It will make the model very well trained on the training data and perform poorly on the test data. We want the model to be well generalized, and for that we add regularization to the cost function that constitutes the objective function. In lot many cases, the loss function is considered an objective function as well. Note: Any cost or loss function can be used instead of L2 loss as shown here. ### **Metrics**. Metrics are used to evaluate the performance of the models during training as well as testing. Since during the evaluation we are not calculating gradients, metric functions are not required to be differentiable. Some of the metrics that are differentiable can be used as loss functions as well, optionally with regularization. Detailed information on these differences by Milos Simic. ## Written by Bhagabat Behera. ## No responses yet.

results.title: Uncertainty propagation in probabilistic seismic loss estimation - ScienceDirect
results.content: One promising approach to the problem, proposed by the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research (PEER) Center, involves breaking the analysis into separate components associated with ground motion hazard, structural response, damage to components and repair costs. Each stage of this method has both inherent (aleatory) randomness and (epistemic) model uncertainty, and these two sources of uncertainty must be propagated through the analysis in order to determine the total uncertainty in the resulting loss estimates. In this paper, the PEER framework for seismic loss estimation is reviewed and options for both characterizing and propagating the various sources of uncertainty are proposed. Current efforts in this field consider the ground motion hazard, building response, damage to building elements, element repair costs, and total repair cost as individual random variables, and then propagate uncertainty through each step to find a final result. This paper provides an overview of the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research (PEER) Center loss estimation framework, and describes approaches for characterizing and propagating the many sources of uncertainty associated with loss estimation. There are several components in this loss estimation model, consisting of quantifying the seismic ground motion hazard, structural response, damage to the building and contents, and resulting consequences (financial losses, fatalities, and business interruption). A procedure for propagating uncertainties in seismic loss estimation has been proposed, utilizing the framework proposed by PEER for performance-based earthquake engineering. The calculation procedure combines inputs of aleatory and epistemic uncertainty in ground motion hazard, building response, damage to building elements, and element repair costs to quantify uncertainty in estimated repair costs and rate of collapse. This study fills this gap by conducting a systematic review covering: the methodological development of regional seismic risk assessment (RSRiA) across its key modules, including hazard analysis, exposure modeling, fragility assessment, and consequence evaluation, as well as the associated uncertainty quantification and propagation; the development of resilience metrics, restoration modeling and planning in regional seismic resilience assessment (RSReA); and the applicability of existing computational workflows. * ### Incorporating modeling uncertainties in the assessment of seismic collapse risk of buildings.

results.title: Ground Truth Data, RAG, and RAG Evaluation Metrics by Baran Akın | Medium
results.content: # Ground Truth Data, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and RAG Evaluation Metrics. ## Introduction. The explosion of AI models, especially in Natural Language Processing (NLP), has led to the evolution of more sophisticated architectures. One such architecture is **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)**, which combines retrieval-based techniques with generative AI models to improve accuracy, reliability, and contextual relevance. However, ensuring the effectiveness of RAG models requires high-quality **ground truth data** and well-defined **evaluation metrics**. In this article, we’ll explore the concept of ground truth data, the working principles of RAG, and the key metrics used to evaluate RAG-based systems. ## What is Ground Truth Data? ### Definition. Ground truth data refers to **accurate, validated, and reliable data** used as a benchmark to train, test, and evaluate machine learning models. It is often collected from real-world sources, expert annotations, or labeled datasets. ### Importance of Ground Truth Data in AI. 1. **Model Training**: Helps AI models learn from high-quality, correct examples. 2. **Evaluation & Validation**: Used as a reference to measure model performance. 3. **Error Analysis**: Enables debugging of model errors by comparing predictions to true values. 4. **Bias Detection**: Identifies biases in…. ## Written by Baran Akın. ## No responses yet.
